What to feed with, and when.
Common problems and how to treat them.
Rich loam with compost, pH 6.0-6.8, free-draining
Half mineral grit, pH 6.0-7.5, never peat-heavy
Cut nitrogen once the first flowers open, or you get a large leafy plant and almost no fruit.
Add calcium and keep watering even: blossom-end rot is a calcium-transport problem caused by drying out, not a disease.
High nitrogen grows tops at the expense of the root. Keep N low and potassium high.
Never use fresh manure - it forks and splits developing roots.
Stop feeding 10-14 days before harvest so nitrates do not accumulate in the leaves.
Cut-and-come-again crops need a light feed after every second harvest, not a heavy one once.
Switch to a high-phosphorus bloom feed as buds form, then back to balanced once flowering ends.
Most flowering houseplants need a cool, unfed rest period to set buds at all - do not feed through it.
No feeding at all from November to February. A fed succulent in low winter light stretches and never recovers its shape.
Pale, stretched new growth means too much nitrogen and too little light, not too little fertiliser.
White crust on the soil or pot rim is fertiliser salt. Flush the pot with plain water until it runs clear.
In a low-light spot halve the dose again - the plant cannot use what it cannot photosynthesise.
Over-feeding gives big, bland leaves. Aromatic oils are strongest in slightly lean soil.
Use a fertiliser cleared for edible crops and observe its harvest interval.
Never feed dry soil - water first, feed 20-30 minutes later, or you will burn the roots.
Do not feed a sick, wilting or pest-infested plant. Feeding a stressed root system makes the damage worse.
Wait 6-8 weeks after repotting: fresh potting mix already contains a starter charge of fertiliser.
Flush the pot with plain water every third month to wash out accumulated salts.
Below 15 degrees C growth stops - stop feeding until it warms up.

string-array.name: tips_fruiting
string-array.item: Fruiting needs 6+ hours of direct light. Under artificial light budget 12-14 hours a day at 20 cm from the leaves.
Water deeply and on a schedule. Alternating drought and flood is what splits fruit and causes blossom-end rot.
Indoors there is no wind and no bees: shake the flowering stems daily, or touch each open flower with a soft brush.
Remove the side shoots that form in the leaf axils of indeterminate varieties, or the plant spends everything on foliage.
Keep night temperature above 13 degrees C. Cold nights abort flowers before you notice anything is wrong.

string-array.name: tips_root
string-array.item: Depth beats width: the container must be deeper than the mature root, or it forks.
Thin seedlings early and ruthlessly. Crowded roots stay pencil-thin no matter how well you feed them.
Stones, clods and fresh manure all cause forked and hairy roots. Sieve the mix.
Keep moisture even. A dry spell followed by a soaking splits the root open.
Mound soil over any shoulder that pushes above the surface, or it goes green and bitter.

string-array.name: tips_leafy
string-array.item: Grows in as little as 4 hours of light, but leaves get thin and pale below that.
Harvest outer leaves and leave the growing point: one plant then crops for weeks.
Heat makes leafy crops bolt and turn bitter. Keep them under 22 degrees C.
Never let the mix dry out completely - one wilt is enough to trigger bolting.
Sow a few seeds every two weeks instead of everything at once, so you always have young leaves.

string-array.name: tips_flowering
string-array.item: Buds form on light. A plant that grows well but never flowers is almost always in a spot that is too dark.
Do not move or rotate the pot once buds have set - most species drop them.
Deadhead spent flowers immediately: seed set switches the plant out of flowering.
Most species need a cool, dry rest of 6-8 weeks to initiate the next flowering.
Water the soil, not the flowers. Water sitting on petals invites grey mould.

string-array.name: tips_succulent
string-array.item: Water hard, then not at all until the mix is dry all the way through. Small sips rot the collar.
Overwatering and underwatering look identical from above. Check the soil, never the leaves.
Stretched, pale growth with widening gaps between leaves means not enough light. It cannot be undone - only cut back.
Move to direct sun gradually over two weeks. A sudden move sunburns the leaves permanently.
Keep it cool and completely dry in winter. That rest is what produces flowers.

string-array.name: tips_foliage
string-array.item: Bright indirect light means a spot where you can read comfortably all day without a lamp, out of direct sun.
Water when the top 3-4 cm are dry. Most losses in this group are drowning, not thirst.
Brown crisp leaf edges mean dry air or salt build-up. Brown soft patches mean too much water.
Dust the leaves monthly. A dusty leaf photosynthesises measurably less.
Rotate the pot a quarter turn every week so it grows evenly rather than leaning.

string-array.name: tips_herb
string-array.item: Pinch out the growing tip early and often - it is what makes the plant bushy instead of leggy.
Never strip more than a third of the plant at one harvest.
Cut flower spikes off as they appear: flowering makes the leaves bitter and coarse.
Most culinary herbs want the sunniest windowsill you have, and slightly lean soil.
Harvest in the morning, when the aromatic oil content is at its peak.
